title: A stock that goes up or down
objectives: Set up a one-step binomial model of a stock.
State and use the no-arbitrage condition $d < 1 + r < u$.

screens.title: A stock that goes up or down
screens.prose: A share costs £100 today. In a year it will be worth one of two prices, and nothing in between. That crude picture is enough to price an option.

screens.title: Two prices in a year
screens.prose: A share costs £100 today. In a year its price is multiplied by $u = 1.2$ if it goes up, or by $d = 0.8$ if it goes down.

state.caption: One step: today, then one year later

screens.question: Fill in the share price in each state in a year.

hints.text: Multiply today’s price by the factor on that branch.
Up multiplies £100 by 1.2.

feedback.correct: £120 if it goes up, £80 if it goes down.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply £100 by the factor on each branch.

byKey.r0c1: Check the up price: $100 \times 1.2$. The factor multiplies the price; it is not added to it.
byKey.r1c1: Check the down price: $100 \times 0.8$. A factor of 0.8 keeps 80% of the price.

explain.text: You multiplied £100 by each factor: £120 up and £80 down. The model allows these two prices and no others. We call it a **one-step binomial tree**.

screens.title: Factors, not returns
screens.prose: We write $S_0 = 100$ for today’s price. The prices in a year are $S_u = uS_0 = 120$ and $S_d = dS_0 = 80$.
screens.question: What return does the share earn in each state?

options.why: You read each factor as the return. The return is the factor minus 1: $1.2 - 1 = 0.2$.
You treated the factors as percentages added to the price. They multiply it: £100 becomes £120.
You took 0.8 as the fall. A factor of 0.8 keeps 80% of the price, so the fall is 20%.

hints.text: How many pounds does the share gain if it goes up?
Up takes £100 to £120.
A gain of £20 on £100 is 20%. The down move loses £20 on £100.

feedback.correct: The return is $u - 1 = 0.2$ up and $d - 1 = -0.2$ down.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each price in a year with £100.

byKey.factor: You read each factor as the return. The return is the factor minus 1: $1.2 - 1 = 0.2$.
byKey.added: You treated the factors as percentages added to the price. They multiply it: £100 becomes £120.

explain.text: The share gains £20 or loses £20 on £100. In general the up return is $u - 1$ and the down return is $d - 1$. So $u$ and $d$ are growth factors, not returns.

screens.title: Share against bond
screens.prose: Lending £100 at a risk-free 5% returns £105 in a year, whatever happens. Move the two factors and compare the share with that loan.
screens.question: What is the largest up factor $u$ at which the share can never end above the loan’s £105?

widget.label: Largest up factor
widget.accept: 1.05, which is $1 + r$: the up price is then £105.

hints.text: Lower $u$ until the up price meets the dashed line.
The dashed line sits at £105.

feedback.correct: At $u = 1.05$ the share’s best case equals the loan.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the $u$ that puts the up price on the dashed £105 line.

byKey.rate: You typed the rate. The factor that matches the loan is $1 + r = 1.05$.
byKey.start: That is where the slider started. At £120 the share can still beat the loan, so lower $u$.

explain.text: At $u = 1.05$ the share ends at £105 at best, the same as the loan, and £80 at worst. Below that, the loan beats the share in every state. Next we turn that into a profit.

screens.title: Short and lend
screens.prose: Suppose $u = 1.04$, so the share ends at £104 or £80. Today you sell a borrowed share for £100 and lend the £100 at 5%. That costs you nothing today.

state.caption: In a year you collect the loan and buy the share back to return it

screens.question: What is your smallest net payoff in a year?

widget.label: Smallest net payoff, in £
widget.accept: £1: $105 - 104$ in the up state. The down state gives £25.

hints.text: In each state, add what you collect and what you pay.
The up state is the tighter one.

feedback.correct: At least £1 in every state, for nothing today.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the net in both states, then take the smaller.

byKey.down: That is the down state, the larger payoff. The smallest is in the up state.
byKey.sign: You collect £105 and pay £104, so the net is positive.
byKey.zero: Lending returns £105 and the buy-back costs at most £104, so you keep at least £1.

explain.text: You end with £1 if up and £25 if down, having paid nothing. A trade that costs nothing, never loses and can gain is an **arbitrage**. Even at $u = 1.05$ it works: £0 up, £25 down.

screens.title: Borrow and buy
screens.prose: Now the share ends at £120 or £108, so $d = 1.08$. The rate is still 5%. You borrow £100 and buy the share.

state.caption: In a year you sell the share and repay the loan with interest

screens.question: What is your smallest net payoff in a year?

hints.text: Which state is worse for a share you own?
The down state is the tighter one.

feedback.correct: Even the down state leaves £3, so this is an arbitrage too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the net in both states, then take the smaller.

byKey.up: That is the up state. The smallest payoff is in the down state.
byKey.no-interest: You repaid £100. The loan grows at 5%, so you owe £105.
byKey.sign: The share is worth £108 and you owe £105, so the net is positive.

explain.text: The worst case, £108, still beats the £105 you owe. When $d \ge 1 + r$ the share beats the loan in every state. Borrowing to buy it is then an arbitrage.

screens.title: A sure bet
screens.prose: Back to £120 or £80, with $r = 5\%$. An analyst says the share rises with probability 0.9. She proposes borrowing £100 at 5% to buy it.
screens.question: Is her trade an arbitrage?

options.text: Yes: it makes money 90% of the time
options.why: You judged the trade by how often it wins. An arbitrage can never lose, and this one loses £25 if the share falls.

options.text: Yes: the expected value, £116, beats the £105 she owes
options.why: You weighted the states by their chances. An expected profit is not a riskless one: the down state still loses £25.

options.text: No: if the share falls she holds £80 and owes £105
No: 0.9 is not high enough to be sure
options.why: You looked for a higher chance. Even at 0.99 the down state loses £25, so no chance below 1 makes it riskless.

hints.text: What does she hold and owe if the share falls?
Look at the down branch.
Down: $80 - 105 = -25$. An arbitrage must not lose in any state.

feedback.correct: The down state loses £25, so the trade is a risk, not an arbitrage.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what happens in the down state.

byKey.ev: You weighted the states by their chances. An expected profit is not a riskless one: the down state still loses £25.
byKey.often: You judged the trade by how often it wins. An arbitrage can never lose, and this one loses £25 if the share falls.

explain.text: Arbitrage is a statement about every state, so the chances never enter. Here $d = 0.8 < 1.05 < 1.2 = u$, so neither trade wins in every state. The chance of up will not matter for pricing either.

screens.title: The arbitrage in general
screens.prose: Suppose $1 + r \ge u$: lending grows at least as fast as the share’s best case. Put the steps of the arbitrage in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Today: sell a borrowed share for $S_0$ and lend the $S_0$ at rate $r$. Net cost 0.
In a year: the loan repays $(1 + r)S_0$.
In a year: buy the share back for $uS_0$ or $dS_0$, never more than $uS_0$.
Net: $(1 + r - u)S_0 \ge 0$ if up and $(1 + r - d)S_0 > 0$ if down, since $d < u$.

hints.text: What happens today comes first.
The net payoff needs both the loan and the buy-back, so it comes last.
Sell and lend today. Collect the loan and buy back in a year. Then subtract.

feedback.correct: Nothing today, never a loss, and a gain if the share falls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with today’s trade and end with the net payoff.

byKey.s4: The net payoff needs both the loan and the buy-back, so it comes last.
byKey.s1: The trade starts today, before anything is repaid.

explain.text: Every state pays at least zero and the down state pays more, for nothing today. The mirror case, $d \ge 1 + r$, flips each step: borrow $S_0$ and buy the share. So a tree without arbitrage needs $d < 1 + r < u$.

screens.title: No free lunch
screens.prose: You found two arbitrages: one when the share’s best case cannot beat lending, one when its worst case beats it. A one-step tree is free of arbitrage exactly when $$d < 1 + r < u.$$
screens.question: With $r = 5\%$, which tree has no arbitrage?

options.why: Here $u < 1.05$: short the share and lend, as on the £104 screen.
Here $d > 1.05$: borrow and buy, as on the £108 screen.
With $u = d$ there is no uncertainty: the share is a bond paying 10%. Borrow at 5% and buy it.

hints.text: Check $d < 1.05 < u$ for each pair.
Only one pair has $d$ below 1.05 and $u$ above it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check $d < 1.05$ and $1.05 < u$ for each pair.

byKey.equal: With $u = d$ there is no uncertainty: the share is a bond paying 10%. Borrow at 5% and buy it.

explain.text: Only $0.9 < 1.05 < 1.15$ meets the condition. When $u = d$ the share is riskless, so it must grow at exactly $1 + r$, or one of the two trades wins. A riskless asset has only one fair growth rate.

screens.title: A bond that may default
screens.prose: A one-year corporate bond pays £100, or £40 if the firm defaults. It trades at £97 today. You can lend risk-free at 5%.

state.caption: Two outcomes, like the share: paid in full or default

screens.question: You sell the bond short for £97 and lend the £97 at 5%. What is your smallest payoff in a year?

hints.text: The loan returns the same amount in both states. Which state costs you more?
If the bond is paid, you must hand over £100.
$97 \times 1.05 = 101.85$, then subtract the £100 you owe the bond’s buyer.

feedback.correct: At least £1.85, for nothing today: the bond is overpriced.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow the £97 at 5%, then subtract the most the bond can pay.

byKey.default: That is the default state, where you hand over only £40. The smallest payoff comes when the bond is paid.
byKey.no-interest: You compared £97 with £100 without interest. The loan returns $97 \times 1.05 = 101.85$.
byKey.sign: Lending returns £101.85 and you pay at most £100, so the payoff is positive.

explain.text: Lending £97 returns £101.85, more than the bond ever pays. Here $u = 100/97 \approx 1.031$, below $1 + r$. Without arbitrage the price must sit between $40/1.05 = \text{£}38.10$ and $100/1.05 = \text{£}95.24$.

ideas: A one-step tree gives the share two prices in a year: $S_u = uS_0$ and $S_d = dS_0$.
An arbitrage costs nothing, never loses and can gain. Whether a trade is one depends on states, not chances.
If $1 + r \ge u$, short the share and lend; if $d \ge 1 + r$, borrow and buy. Otherwise there is no arbitrage.

formula.name: No arbitrage on a one-step tree
formula.note: $u$ and $d$ multiply the price; the returns are $u - 1$ and $d - 1$.

summary.trap: A trade that wins 90% of the time is a bet, not an arbitrage. Check the worst state.

quiz.question: What is the share worth in a year if it goes up?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply today’s price by the up factor.

byKey.added: You added 1.25 to £40. The factor multiplies the price.
byKey.return: That is the gain, £10. The question asks for the price.

options.why: Here $0.95 < 1.03 < 1.1$, so neither trade wins in every state.
Here $0.8 < 1.03 < 1.2$. A wide tree is risky, not an arbitrage.
Here $1.0 < 1.03 < 1.05$. The share can still fall short of the loan.

quiz.prose: A share costs £100 and $u = d = 1.02$: it ends at £102 whatever happens. The risk-free rate is 5%.
quiz.question: You sell a borrowed share and lend the £100. What do you make in a year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Collect the loan, then buy the share back.

byKey.sign: The loan returns £105 and the share costs £102, so you gain.
byKey.rate: You kept the whole £5 of interest. You must also buy the share back for £102, not £100.
byKey.none: With $u = d$ the share is a bond paying 2%. Lending at 5% beats it by £3.

explain.text: With $u = d$ the share carries no risk, so it is a bond paying 2%. Lending pays 5%, so selling the share and lending earns £3 for certain.

quiz.prose: A share trades at £50 before an earnings announcement. After the results it will trade at £60 or at £42.
quiz.question: Which factors describe the move as a one-step tree?

options.why: You assumed the fall mirrors the rise. $42/50 = 0.84$, a fall of 16%.
Those are the returns. The factors are 1 plus each return.
Those are the moves in pounds. A factor is the new price over the old.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each price after the results by £50.

explain.text: Each factor is the new price over today’s: $60/50 = 1.2$ and $42/50 = 0.84$. The tree need not be symmetric.
